stories.headline: FCIK welcomes Shahjehan Khan’s election as President Zainakote Industries Association
stories.title: FCIK welcomes Shahjehan Khan’s election as President Zainakote Industries Association
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 27: The Federation of Chambers of Industries Kashmir (FCIK) has congratulated Shahjehan Khan on his election as President of the Small Scale Industries Association, Zainakote. Khan defeated Mohammad Ayub in a straight contest, while young entrepreneur Imran Bashir was elected General Secretary. The elections were conducted by an Election Commission headed by Umar Mukhtar Bhat. Welcoming the outcome, FCIK Advisory Committee Head Shahid Kamili said the election of an experienced entrepreneur with sound judgment was particularly significant at a time when Kashmir’s industrial sector was confronting serious challenges. He expressed hope that Khan would bring his practical experience to bear on the concerns of industrial units in Zainakote and contribute to the broader work of FCIK, of which the Association is an affiliate. Khan is the Managing Director of Hyacinth Agro Products Pvt. Ltd., with business interests spanning food processing and preservation, cold-chain infrastructure, bakery and confectionery, food and beverages, refrigerated logistics and allied agro-industries. His business philosophy centres on farmer empowerment, employment generation, import substitution, local manufacturing and taking Kashmir’s rich agricultural produce to national and international markets. Khan has been actively involved in the Association’s affairs and has previously held various positions within the Association and FCIK. Established in the late 1970s, Zainakote is among Kashmir’s oldest industrial estates. Spread over 525 kanals, the estate houses 217 industrial units. Former FCIK presidents Abdul Majid Khan, Meraj ud Din Qureshi, Shakeel Qalander, Zahoor Ahmad Bhat and Mohammad Ashraf Mir also welcomed Khan’s election and extended their best wishes to the new team. Congratulating Khan and his colleagues, the former presidents said the time had come for a new generation of capable entrepreneurs to take up leadership roles in industrial associations and their apex chamber. They said entrepreneurs with experience in running successful enterprises had a practical understanding of the challenges faced by the industrial community and could use that insight to advocate simpler procedures, improved market access and support for stressed units seeking to resume production. Congratulatory messages have also poured in from presidents and members of industrial associations across Kashmir, including those representing Baghi Ali Mardan Khan, Zakura, Shalteng, Baramulla, Sopore, Kupwara, Pulwama, Khunmoh, Rangreth, Sanat Nagar, Lassipora, Anchidora, Vessu, Bijbehara and Ganderbal, besides district presidents.

stories.headline: Global South and Climate Justice
stories.title: Global South and Climate Justice
stories.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs website proudly and prominently mentions these words of Prime Minister Narendra Modi from his address to the 18th BRICS summit which was held in September this year under his chairship in Delhi “The Global South is today in the front row of global crises, but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this “pyramid of privilege” into a “platform of partnership”, where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and the advancement of humanity remains at the heart of every endeavour”. It has been India’s constant desire that the international system should be democratic and work for the welfare of the poor and underprivileged countries and peoples. It has championed the causes of the Global South and Modi has strongly moved in that direction too. But the sad fact is that the world order, put in place after the Second World War by the victors of that war, is essentially undemocratic. It has remained so for more than eighty years. Hence, the question is whether Modi’s aspiration will ever get translated into reality. Or, is the Global South consigned to play little or no role in decision making on issues which are vital for its future. Apart from the desire of the advanced countries to retain rules making powers for inter-state relations and thus deny the Global South a role in this area, the absence of consensus within it on some vital global matters hampers it from pressing its case for eroding the “pyramid of privilege”. Once again this came to the fore in the Conference of Parties (COP) 31st meeting of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) which concluded earlier this week in Turkiye without a main outcome document. This was one of the few occasions when a COP meeting ended on this note. This was not a good augury for finding a resolution for the principal existential crisis facing humanity–that of climate change. In any event, as this writer has noted in these columns, the absence of the US from the UNFCCC makes it weak. This is because the US is one of the highest emitters of greenhouse gases (GHG The principal reason for the collapse of COP 31 was the failure of the parties to reach an agreement on the phasing out of fossil fuels. On the one side were some advanced countries and some developing island states which favoured an aggressive approach while on the other were countries, including India, which wanted a realistic attitude and not to mention a phase out of fossil fuels. The Indian statement focused on the real causes of climate change. Bhupinder Yadav, Minister for Environment put it well when he said ““Our planet is warmer today. The cause is the industrialisation and economic growth of some, fuelled over two centuries by unabated greenhouse gas emissions. To now expect the Global South to bear the burden of addressing the consequences of their past actions in the name of ‘higher ambition’ is unjustified’. He also correctly remarked “Developing countries cannot be asked to choose between climate action and the legitimate right to development, to decent living standards, health and education. Equitable access to the remaining, depleted, carbon budget is non-negotiable”. Yadav’s words were justified for countries like India but small island countries like Maldives or some in the South Pacific fear that even a little rise in sea levels because of global warming would lead to their doom. It is this survival instinct which compels them not to heed the call for climate justice that countries like India push for. These divergent interests in the ranks of the Global South are exploited by advanced countries to break its unity. That is one point that Modi could have addressed in his BRICS address and that leads to the diplomatic task that India could perform. This relates to seriously embarking on an exercise to create a unity in Global South countries on major issues which will increase their bargaining power. Another objective that India could lead is to increase the fund of scientific and technical capacities of these countries. One obvious way of creating unity in the Global South on climate change because of global warming, is to focus on the need of the advanced world to adhere to their pledges on adaptation and mitigation. Indeed, India could suggest that a larger per capita proportion of this assistance could be given to island countries because the threat they face is existential. Besides, they have small populations and that forward looking international conventions must be framed for their welfare and rehabilitation, including political, in different parts of the world. This concern is not based on an unrealistic scenario for a rise of even a metre in sea levels could submerge some island countries in the South Pacific which are really a string of atolls. As it is India has a dialogue with the South Pacific Forum. The idea expressed here could be refined and taken forward to ensure that the unity of the Global South on climate change is restored. Another area where India could build on is to imaginatively share its expertise with the Global South in applications relating to AI which are being developed here. Such cooperation will be in keeping with the tradition established in the early years of its independence when Indian experts went out to developing countries to share Indian experiences and developing countries students came here to study. Now the circumstances have changed but new ways have to be found to take that process forward.

stories.title: Beyond the business: Colonel Manbeer Choudhary's idea of leadership and the responsibility to give back

opening: Leadership is often judged by what an individual builds, the organisations they lead and the professional milestones they achieve.
But there is another dimension to leadership that deserves equal attention: what an individual does with the opportunities and resources that success brings.
body: For Colonel Manbeer Choudhary, this responsibility has been a consistent part of his journey.
A retired Indian Army officer, hospitality entrepreneur and philanthropist, he has moved across very different professional worlds while retaining a commitment to service.
His work in healthcare, children's welfare, support for war widows and ex servicemen, and charitable initiatives reflects a belief that professional achievement should create value beyond business.
A Foundation Built on Discipline and ServiceColonel Manbeer's outlook was shaped by his upbringing in a Jatt Sikh family with ancestral roots in Gujranwala.
His family migrated during the Partition of India, and his mother, Mrs Jaswant Kaur, took up teaching to support the family.
Her perseverance and commitment to education left a lasting impression on him.
After studying at a government aided school in Karnal, he joined the National Defence Academy and served in the Indian Army for 25 years.
The experience shaped his understanding of discipline, accountability, leadership and collective responsibility.
His decision to leave the Army to attend to his ailing father marked a significant transition.
He subsequently entered hospitality, beginning with Jewels Hotel in Karnal.

What followed was an entrepreneurial journey that led to the establishment of Noormahal Palace, now Noor Mahal by Marriott International, India's first Autograph Collection hotel, along with Hazuri Bagh in Karnal and Colonel Saab, with restaurants in London's Holborn and Trafalgar Square.
His contribution to the hospitality sector also included institutional leadership.
He served as President of the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India during 2005 and 2006 and as Founder President of the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Haryana.
Yet, beyond these professional milestones, his engagement with social welfare has remained a defining part of his work.
Philanthropy with a Focus on Dignity and OpportunityColonel Manbeer Choudhary's philanthropic activities span healthcare, education, nourishment and the welfare of disadvantaged communities.
He has supported charitable organisations, orphanages and institutions working with children with hearing and speech impairments.
An important part of this commitment is his association with MDD Bal Bhawan, where he has taken responsibility for supporting the orphanage initiative.
As its Founder and Trustee, his involvement reflects a commitment to children's welfare and the belief that every child deserves care, dignity and an opportunity to build a better future.
His social engagement also extends to the armed forces community.
Through his association with the Army Wives Welfare Association (AWWA), he has supported war widows through financial assistance and helped create employment opportunities.
He has also provided employment opportunities to ex servicemen in the region.
These efforts address an important aspect of social welfare: helping individuals and families who have faced difficult circumstances regain stability, dignity and economic independence.
During the COVID 19 pandemic, his hospitality establishments extended accommodation, meals and medical assistance to patients and doctors.
His support for educational initiatives, including providing computers to schools, further demonstrates his interest in practical interventions that improve access to opportunity.
The Sikh Identity and the Principle of SevaColonel Manbeer's Jatt Sikh identity is central to his personal and cultural heritage.
His family's roots in Gujranwala connect him to a region deeply associated with Sikh history, including the Sukerchakia Misl and Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
The Sikh principle of seva, or selfless service, has particular relevance to his approach to philanthropy.
For him, community responsibility is not simply an expression of identity; it is reflected in active participation, charitable contributions and support for institutions working for social welfare.
His contributions to charitable and community causes have received recognition from Gurdwara Prabandhak Committees, including HGPC, and international Sikh forums on several occasions.
These recognitions acknowledge his engagement with social welfare and his contributions within the wider Sikh community.
His work reflects an understanding that community development requires sustained involvement and a willingness to support people and institutions beyond one's immediate professional responsibilities.

A Broader Measure of SuccessColonel Manbeer Choudhary's journey brings together three distinct forms of contribution: service to the nation, institution building through entrepreneurship and service to society through philanthropy.
His military career established a foundation of discipline and duty.
His hospitality ventures demonstrated the ability to adapt and build in an unfamiliar industry.
His charitable work has provided another expression of leadership, one centred on the welfare of children, vulnerable families, war widows, ex servicemen and underserved communities.
In an environment where business success is frequently measured through scale and financial performance, his journey offers a broader perspective.
The value of an institution can also be understood through the opportunities it creates and the communities it supports.
For Colonel Manbeer, the idea of service has simply evolved with time.
It began in uniform, continued through entrepreneurship and finds expression today in philanthropy and community welfare.
His enduring contribution lies not only in the institutions he has helped build, but in his belief that the responsibility to serve society must remain an integral part of leadership.

stories.headline: Why Kashmir must heed the Uttarakhand warning
stories.title: Why Kashmir must heed the Uttarakhand warning
stories.summary: Viral videos showing heavy earthmoving machines cutting into the fragile shoreline of Sheshnag Lake in upper Pahalgam have sparked deep environmental concern across Jammu and Kashmir. Located at around 11,780 feet, this excavation is not a routine project, but a serious threat to the ecological and water security of South Kashmir. Objections from the Kashmiri Pandit community and civil society groups also highlight the religious and cultural value of this alpine landscape. Subjecting a sensitive glacial lake to heavy mechanical digging ignores both its ecological fragility and spiritual sanctity. In its defence, the Border Roads Organisation stated that the machinery is widening and stabilising existing tracks, easing Amarnath Yatra congestion, and following environmental safeguards. While improving pilgrim access and managing crowds are valid administrative goals, the methods used must respect mountain geology. High altitude terrain comprises unstable glacial deposits, loose moraines, permafrost, and steep slopes that fail easily when disturbed. Heavy excavation without scientific assessment worsens erosion, weakens slopes, and alters natural water channels. An ecosystem cannot be stabilised by weakening its geological foundation. Experiences across the Indian Himalayan Region offer clear warnings. The Kedarnath disaster and land subsidence in Joshimath exposed the heavy cost of development that exceeds natural limits. Uttarakhand has since faced intense scrutiny over carrying capacity, crowd management, and construction in fragile zones. These lessons must guide planning across the Himalayan arc, including Kashmir. The real question is not whether pilgrims need better facilities, but whether they can be provided without harming the natural systems sustaining entire populations. The danger at Sheshnag is acute because of its location within the upper Lidder glacial landscape. Experts have listed Sheshnag among 14 high risk glacial lakes in Jammu and Kashmir prone to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods. Such floods occur when natural barriers holding back glacial water suddenly fail. Disturbing moraines, altering drainage channels, or weakening nearby slopes increases existing risks. Devastating glacial lake floods in Sikkim and other Himalayan regions demonstrate why preventive action must precede environmental damage. The consequences extend well beyond the lake's shores. Together with the neighbouring Kolahoi glacier system, the Sheshnag basin feeds the upper Lidder River, which flows through Pahalgam and Bijbehara before joining the Jhelum near village Gur. This river is indispensable for drinking water, irrigation, farming, and South Kashmir's wider economy. Its waters support extensive paddy cultivation, horticulture, local trade, and tourism across Pahalgam, Bijbehara, Anantnag East, and nearby areas. Weakening this upper catchment threatens a shared resource supporting thousands of households. Scientific evidence makes these concerns urgent. Research led by noted Earth scientist Professor Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, Vice Chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology in Awantipora, highlights the rapid retreat of regional glaciers. In a 2020 study of 147 glaciers across the Kashmir Himalaya, including the Lidder, Vishav, Doodhganga, and Sind basins of the Jhelum River, Romshoo and colleagues found a 28.82 percent area loss between 1980 and 2018, shrinking from 101.73 square kilometres to 72.41 square kilometres. Mapping South Kashmir glaciers like Kolahoi, Hoksar, and Wokhalbal, the study revealed that smaller glaciers under one square kilometre lost 41.20 percent of their area compared to 15.97 percent for larger glaciers above three square kilometres, while fragmentation split 11 glaciers and raised the mapped count from 147 to 153. Complementing these findings, a 2020 study by Irfan Rashid and colleagues on the Kolahoi Glacier documented a 23.6 percent area loss between 1962 and 2018, with retreat rates tripling after 2000. Their research shows shrinking ice has significantly reduced Lidder River flows at Aru, Gur, and Kirkadal, pushing downstream farmers to cut water intensive rice paddy cultivation by 39 percent while orchards and built up areas expanded sharply. Rising temperatures alongside vehicular emissions, ambient black carbon, pilgrim crowds, waste, and excavation place severe stress on this corridor, reflected in the premature melting of the natural ice lingam and eroding slopes. The legal framework is equally clear. The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have consistently stressed precaution, scientific scrutiny, and accountability in ecologically sensitive zones. Under the Precautionary Principle, authorities must prevent serious or irreversible environmental harm even when scientific uncertainty persists. Any major alteration around Sheshnag must follow transparent environmental appraisal, geological and glaciological studies, and statutory clearances. Administrative promises of safeguards cannot replace independent scientific verification. The administration need not choose between pilgrimage and environmental protection. Both can coexist if development respects natural carrying capacity. Heavy mechanical digging in the Sheshnag and upper Lidder catchments must stop immediately until independent glaciologists, geologists, and environmental scientists evaluate slope stability, moraine integrity, drainage patterns, downstream flood exposure, and cumulative ecological impacts. Their findings must enter the public domain to guide a strict carrying capacity framework and monitoring system. A pilgrimage acquires deeper meaning when nature is protected rather than sacrificed for convenience. The Himalayas are living ecosystems, not endless construction sites, sustaining rivers, agriculture, biodiversity, and communities far beyond their boundaries. Uttarakhand has paid a heavy price for overlooking these limits, and Kashmir must not repeat those mistakes. Safeguarding this fragile landscape is inseparable from protecting South Kashmir's water security and future generations. The author is a serving legislator from South Kashmir’s Bijbehara constituency and contributes occasionally on public policy and governance.

Uttarakhand has since faced intense scrutiny over carrying capacity, crowd management, and construction in fragile zones.
These lessons must guide planning across the Himalayan arc, including Kashmir.
The real question is not whether pilgrims need better facilities, but whether they can be provided without harming the natural systems sustaining entire populations.
The danger at Sheshnag is acute because of its location within the upper Lidder glacial landscape.
Experts have listed Sheshnag among 14 high risk glacial lakes in Jammu and Kashmir prone to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods.
Such floods occur when natural barriers holding back glacial water suddenly fail.
Disturbing moraines, altering drainage channels, or weakening nearby slopes increases existing risks.
Devastating glacial lake floods in Sikkim and other Himalayan regions demonstrate why preventive action must precede environmental damage.
The consequences extend well beyond the lake's shores.
Together with the neighbouring Kolahoi glacier system, the Sheshnag basin feeds the upper Lidder River, which flows through Pahalgam and Bijbehara before joining the Jhelum near village Gur.
This river is indispensable for drinking water, irrigation, farming, and South Kashmir's wider economy.
Its waters support extensive paddy cultivation, horticulture, local trade, and tourism across Pahalgam, Bijbehara, Anantnag East, and nearby areas.
Weakening this upper catchment threatens a shared resource supporting thousands of households.
Scientific evidence makes these concerns urgent.

Research led by noted Earth scientist Professor Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, Vice Chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology in Awantipora, highlights the rapid retreat of regional glaciers.

In a 2020 study of 147 glaciers across the Kashmir Himalaya, including the Lidder, Vishav, Doodhganga, and Sind basins of the Jhelum River, Romshoo and colleagues found a 28.82 percent area loss between 1980 and 2018, shrinking from 101.73 square kilometres to 72.41 square kilometres.

Rising temperatures alongside vehicular emissions, ambient black carbon, pilgrim crowds, waste, and excavation place severe stress on this corridor, reflected in the premature melting of the natural ice lingam and eroding slopes.
The legal framework is equally clear.
The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have consistently stressed precaution, scientific scrutiny, and accountability in ecologically sensitive zones.
Under the Precautionary Principle, authorities must prevent serious or irreversible environmental harm even when scientific uncertainty persists.
Any major alteration around Sheshnag must follow transparent environmental appraisal, geological and glaciological studies, and statutory clearances.
Administrative promises of safeguards cannot replace independent scientific verification.
The administration need not choose between pilgrimage and environmental protection.
Both can coexist if development respects natural carrying capacity.

Heavy mechanical digging in the Sheshnag and upper Lidder catchments must stop immediately until independent glaciologists, geologists, and environmental scientists evaluate slope stability, moraine integrity, drainage patterns, downstream flood exposure, and cumulative ecological impacts.
Their findings must enter the public domain to guide a strict carrying capacity framework and monitoring system.
A pilgrimage acquires deeper meaning when nature is protected rather than sacrificed for convenience.
The Himalayas are living ecosystems, not endless construction sites, sustaining rivers, agriculture, biodiversity, and communities far beyond their boundaries.
Uttarakhand has paid a heavy price for overlooking these limits, and Kashmir must not repeat those mistakes.
Safeguarding this fragile landscape is inseparable from protecting South Kashmir's water security and future generations.
The author is a serving legislator from South Kashmir’s Bijbehara constituency and contributes occasionally on public policy and governance.

stories.headline: Chief Justice Bhati highlights enduring strength of Constitution
stories.title: Chief Justice Bhati highlights enduring strength of Constitution
stories.summary: Jammu, Nov 27: Commemorating 77 years of the adoption of the Constitution of India and reaffirming the collective commitment to its cherished ideals of Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, the Jammu & Kashmir Legal Services Authority, in collaboration with the High Court Legal Services Committee and District Legal Services Authority, Jammu, on Friday observed Constitution Day, 2026 at Police Auditorium, Gulshan Ground, here. The programme was graced by Dr Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice, High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh and Patron-in-Chief, J&K Legal Services Authority, as the chief guest, in presence of Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Sanjay Parihar, Justice Yash Paul Bourney, Judges, High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Jammu. The programme was aimed at rekindling constitutional consciousness among the masses, fostering respect for the supremacy of the Constitution and instilling a sense of responsible citizenship, particularly among the younger generation. It also sought to emphasize that preservation of constitutional democracy is a shared responsibility of institutions and citizens alike. In his presidential address, Chief Justice, through an engaging interaction with the students and several real-life illustrations, elaborated upon the three dimensions of justice i.e social, economic and political, as enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution. Highlighting the equal value of every citizen’s vote irrespective of their social or economic standing, Dr Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, underscored the remarkable achievement of political equality while emphasizing the need for sustained efforts towards social and economic equality and securing a dignified life for every individual. Referring to the constitutional foresight of its framers, Chief Justice highlighted how Article 395 severed the remaining constitutional links with colonial rule and emphasized that the inherent flexibility of the Constitution is its greatest strength, binding the country’s vast geographical, cultural and social diversity into a unified national fabric. Reflecting upon the rich judicial heritage of Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, Chief Justice made a special reference to the establishment of the High Court in 1928, which is now approaching its centenary, as a reflection of the region’s deep-rooted constitutional values.

stories.headline: Union Cabinet clears revised bills on delimitation, women’s quota
stories.title: Union Cabinet clears revised bills on delimitation, women’s quota
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 27: The Union Cabinet on Friday approved a revised legislative proposal for delimitation and implementation of women's reservation, providing for a uniform 50 percent increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats across all states while retaining their existing proportion of parliamentary representation until 2051, national media reports said. The decision, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, comes ahead of the special session of Parliament scheduled to begin on November 30, during which the government is expected to introduce the revised legislation. The four-day session is likely to conclude on December 3. The revised proposal seeks to address objections raised by Opposition parties, particularly those from southern states, over the potential impact of population-based delimitation on the regional balance of political representation. Under the new formula, every state would receive a uniform 50 percent increase in its existing Lok Sabha seats, ensuring that its proportionate share in the House does not change. The existing inter-state share of representation would remain protected until 2051. According to the proposed Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, a new provision has been introduced for a 50 percent increase in the number of seats to facilitate the immediate implementation of reservation for women under Article 334A of the Constitution. The government has also proposed withdrawing the earlier Delimitation Bill, 2026, pending in the Lok Sabha, as the replacement legislation substantially alters its provisions. The revised framework is aimed at facilitating implementation of the 33 percent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha from the 2029 general elections. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju has said the government would introduce the Bill in the Lok Sabha on November 30 and urged Opposition parties to participate in the debate. The fresh move follows the defeat of the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill in the Lok Sabha on April 17. The legislation, which sought to increase the Lok Sabha's strength from the existing 543 to a maximum of 850 members, secured 298 votes in favour and 230 against, falling short of the two-thirds majority required for a constitutional amendment. The government subsequently withdrew two related Bills concerning delimitation and the extension of the proposed changes to Union Territories. The earlier legislation had proposed setting up a delimitation commission to redraw parliamentary constituencies based on the latest published Census figures. Opposition parties, particularly those representing southern states, had argued that such an exercise could increase the political weight of northern states at the expense of states that had successfully controlled population growth. The revised proposal is expected to address these concerns by retaining the existing proportional representation of states while providing for a uniform increase in the number of seats. Former Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and DMK president M K Stalin has reiterated that his party would not compromise on its two principal demands: that Tamil Nadu's existing 7.18 percent share in the Lok Sabha should not decline and that the proportion of parliamentary representation among states, based on the 1971 Census, should remain frozen for another 25 years. Stalin has maintained that there has been no change in the DMK's position and ruled out any compromise on the issue. However, the party's two principal demands have been incorporated into the revised proposal. The Cabinet decision assumes significance as the NDA does not have the two-thirds majority on its own required to pass a constitutional amendment. Support from parties outside the ruling alliance will therefore be crucial for the legislation to pass Parliament. Political parties have begun preparing their strategies ahead of the special session. The Shiv Sena has issued a whip directing its MPs to remain present in Parliament. The INDIA bloc is scheduled to hold a meeting in New Delhi on Saturday, November 28, at 11:30 am. The DMK is also expected to hold a separate meeting on Saturday morning to discuss the proposed legislation. Amid preparations by Opposition parties, speculation has also been rife within NDA ranks over the government's ability to secure the required numbers. Reports suggest the ruling alliance is confident of getting the revised legislation passed. (With ANI Inputs)

stories.headline: Navy receives final Project 17A frigate Vindhyagiri, completing seven-ship programme
stories.title: Navy receives final Project 17A frigate Vindhyagiri, completing seven-ship programme
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 27: The Indian Navy on Friday received Vindhyagiri, the seventh and final Nilgiri-class (Project 17A) frigate, from Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers Ltd (GRSE) in Kolkata, marking the completion of deliveries of all seven ships under the programme. The delivery of Yard 3024 Vindhyagiri on November 27 also marks a milestone in India’s indigenous warship design and construction capabilities. It is the third Project 17A frigate built by GRSE. Designed by the Warship Design Bureau, Project 17A frigates are multi-mission platforms equipped with advanced weapons and sensors, enhancing their capabilities in anti-air, anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare. Named after the Vindhyagiri mountain range in Karnataka, the ship is a reincarnation of the erstwhile INS Vindhyagiri, a Leander-class frigate which served the Navy for 31 years, from July 8, 1981, to June 11, 2012. All seven Project 17A frigates have been delivered within 23 months of the delivery of the first ship, INS Nilgiri, on December 20, 2024. The construction period of Vindhyagiri was reduced to 68 months, compared to 84 months taken for the first-of-class ship.

stories.headline: IPL 2027: Rohit Sharma to Captain Mumbai Indians
stories.title: IPL 2027: Rohit Sharma to Captain Mumbai Indians
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 27: Mumbai Indians on Friday announced that Rohit Sharma will captain the team, going into the 2027 IPL season. As the franchise prepares to celebrate its landmark 20th season, one of its most loved and successful leaders will lead the Blue and Gold into an exciting new chapter. Rohit’s journey with Mumbai Indians has been a special one. Since joining the franchise in 2011, he has been at the heart of some of its greatest moments, leading MI to five IPL titles and helping shape the team’s winning culture. His leadership, belief in young talent and deep connection with the Paltan have made him an integral part of the Mumbai Indians story. As per a statement issued, Nita M. Ambani said: “We bid for Rohit in 2011, and from that moment, he became part of our Mumbai Indians family. I still remember the young Rohit who joined us, and it has been such a joy and privilege to watch him grow over the years as a cricketer, a champion, a leader, and a wonderful family man.” “As we celebrate the 20th season of Mumbai Indians, it is a very special moment for all of us to see Rohit lead the team once again. He has given us so many wonderful memories over the years, and I know how much he means to our Paltan. I hope this new chapter brings many more moments of pride for him, for our team and for the millions of fans who love Mumbai Indians. Rohit, we are all cheering for you!” Akash Ambani said: “I am delighted to have Rohit lead the Blue and Gold into our landmark 20th season. The bond that Rohit shares with Mumbai Indians and our Paltan is truly special. In our conversations about the season ahead, there was a shared sense of excitement and ambition for what we can achieve together.” Rohit Sharma, Captain, Mumbai Indians, said: “Mumbai Indians has been a huge part of my life, and leading this team has always been something I have always taken great pride in. The conversations with Nita Bhabhi and Akash about the season ahead have been exciting, and I have a lot of belief in what we can achieve.”

stories.headline: Govt seeks special centre package as J&K faces up to 1,300 MW winter power gap
stories.title: Govt seeks special centre package as J&K faces up to 1,300 MW winter power gap
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 27: Jammu and Kashmir Minister for Power Development Department (PDD), Revenue, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Disaster Management, Relief, Rehabilitation and Reconstruction (DMRRR) and Elections, Ali Mohammad Sagar, has sought a dedicated financial package from the Centre to address the power sector’s infrastructure gaps and growing winter demand. Sagar raised the issue during the State Ministers’ Conference on Power in New Delhi, chaired by Union Power Minister Manohar Lal, where he interacted with the Group of Ministers and submitted a detailed memorandum outlining Jammu and Kashmir’s power-sector requirements. The memorandum seeks financial assistance for comprehensive modernisation of the sector, strengthening of transmission and distribution networks, reduction of power losses, expansion of hydropower generation and improved electricity availability, particularly during winter. Highlighting the region’s geographical and climatic challenges, Sagar said Jammu and Kashmir’s mountainous terrain, scattered habitations and remote locations made the development and maintenance of power infrastructure particularly difficult. He said heavy snowfall, avalanches, landslides, cloudbursts and flash floods frequently damage electricity infrastructure, while winter demand rises sharply as hydropower generation declines. Sagar highlighted improvements in the financial and operational performance of Jammu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (JPDCL) and Kashmir Power Distribution Corporation Limited (KPDCL). Revenue realisation by the two distribution companies has increased from approximately Rs 3,060 crore in 2021-22 to Rs 5,290 crore in 2025-26, registering growth of nearly 73 per cent, he said. AT&C losses have also declined, from 49.82 per cent to 27.13 per cent in JPDCL and from 65.61 per cent to 33 per cent in KPDCL. The gap between the average cost of supply and average revenue realised has also narrowed substantially. Under the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), 14.07 lakh smart meters have been sanctioned, of which nearly 12.25 lakh had been installed as of November 19, 2026. Distribution strengthening and loss-reduction works worth Rs 4,708.52 crore have also been sanctioned, with substantial physical progress reported in both distribution companies. The Minister sought continued Central assistance for replacing ageing and overloaded transformers, augmenting 33/11 kV infrastructure, installing additional substations, strengthening low-tension networks and developing alternate feeding arrangements. He also stressed the need for underground and insulated cabling in vulnerable areas and dedicated enforcement wings to curb power theft and unauthorised consumption. Drawing attention to the winter power scenario, Sagar said Jammu and Kashmir’s peak demand during the previous winter had touched approximately 3,362 MW, comprising 1,456 MW in Jammu and 1,906 MW in Kashmir. The anticipated restricted demand for winter 2026-27 is around 3,450 MW, with the estimated supply gap ranging between 600 MW and 1,300 MW. He urged the Centre to provide additional unallocated power, ensure predictable allocations and continue or enhance the additional 329 MW allocation for December 2026 to February 2027. Sagar also sought support for affordable long-term power procurement and banking arrangements with neighbouring states, including Punjab and Uttar Pradesh. On hydropower development, the Minister said Jammu and Kashmir had an estimated potential of 14,635 MW, of which around 3,540 MW had been harnessed so far. He highlighted the ongoing Pakal Dul, Kiru, Kwar and Ratle projects, with an aggregate capacity of approximately 3,563.5 MW, and said the Government aimed to increase installed hydropower capacity to around 10,975.65 MW by 2035. Sagar sought Central assistance through grants, concessional financing and viability gap funding to accelerate hydropower projects, undertake geological investigations and prepare detailed project reports. He also highlighted the proposed Jammu and Kashmir Hydro Power Policy 2026 and the need to encourage private investment in the sector. The Minister underlined the importance of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in managing peak demand and integrating renewable energy into the power grid. He outlined a proposal to develop 250 MW/1,000 MWh of storage capacity over three years and scale it up to 1,000 MW/4,000 MWh over five years, up to 2031. On transmission infrastructure, Sagar highlighted the ongoing transformation of the Jammu and Kashmir Power Transmission Corporation Limited (JKPTCL), which has a transformation capacity of approximately 12,875 MVA, with another 3,766 MVA in the pipeline. He sought support for new transmission lines, grid substations, transformer augmentation, modern digital substations and strengthening of transmission corridors to meet future demand. Sagar stressed the need to make power infrastructure more resilient to natural disasters and proposed a dedicated Himalayan Power Infrastructure Resilience Programme. The proposal includes procurement of Emergency Restoration System (ERS) units. While seven units have already been procured for Jammu, he highlighted the requirement for 15 additional units for Jammu and 10 for Kashmir. Calling for greater investment in digitalisation and capacity building, the Minister emphasised smart-grid technologies, cybersecurity, modern operational systems and specialised training for power-sector personnel. He proposed establishing two dedicated Power Training Colleges, one each in the Jammu and Kashmir divisions. Sagar said reliable and affordable electricity was essential for supporting industrial growth, tourism, horticulture, cold-chain infrastructure, healthcare facilities and the emerging electric mobility ecosystem in Jammu and Kashmir. He urged the Centre to consider a dedicated Jammu and Kashmir Power Sector Development and Modernisation Package, combining grants, concessional loans, viability gap funding and project-based assistance. The Minister also proposed constitution of a joint working group comprising representatives of the Government of India and Jammu and Kashmir to examine the proposals and facilitate their time-bound implementation.

The Minister sought continued Central assistance for replacing ageing and overloaded transformers, augmenting 33/11 kV infrastructure, installing additional substations, strengthening low-tension networks and developing alternate feeding arrangements.
He also stressed the need for underground and insulated cabling in vulnerable areas and dedicated enforcement wings to curb power theft and unauthorised consumption.

Drawing attention to the winter power scenario, Sagar said Jammu and Kashmir’s peak demand during the previous winter had touched approximately 3,362 MW, comprising 1,456 MW in Jammu and 1,906 MW in Kashmir.
The anticipated restricted demand for winter 2026-27 is around 3,450 MW, with the estimated supply gap ranging between 600 MW and 1,300 MW.
He urged the Centre to provide additional unallocated power, ensure predictable allocations and continue or enhance the additional 329 MW allocation for December 2026 to February 2027.
Sagar also sought support for affordable long-term power procurement and banking arrangements with neighbouring states, including Punjab and Uttar Pradesh.
On hydropower development, the Minister said Jammu and Kashmir had an estimated potential of 14,635 MW, of which around 3,540 MW had been harnessed so far.

He highlighted the ongoing Pakal Dul, Kiru, Kwar and Ratle projects, with an aggregate capacity of approximately 3,563.5 MW, and said the Government aimed to increase installed hydropower capacity to around 10,975.65 MW by 2035.

Sagar sought Central assistance through grants, concessional financing and viability gap funding to accelerate hydropower projects, undertake geological investigations and prepare detailed project reports.
He also highlighted the proposed Jammu and Kashmir Hydro Power Policy 2026 and the need to encourage private investment in the sector.
The Minister underlined the importance of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in managing peak demand and integrating renewable energy into the power grid.
He outlined a proposal to develop 250 MW/1,000 MWh of storage capacity over three years and scale it up to 1,000 MW/4,000 MWh over five years, up to 2031.

On transmission infrastructure, Sagar highlighted the ongoing transformation of the Jammu and Kashmir Power Transmission Corporation Limited (JKPTCL), which has a transformation capacity of approximately 12,875 MVA, with another 3,766 MVA in the pipeline.
He sought support for new transmission lines, grid substations, transformer augmentation, modern digital substations and strengthening of transmission corridors to meet future demand.
Sagar stressed the need to make power infrastructure more resilient to natural disasters and proposed a dedicated Himalayan Power Infrastructure Resilience Programme.
The proposal includes procurement of Emergency Restoration System (ERS) units.
While seven units have already been procured for Jammu, he highlighted the requirement for 15 additional units for Jammu and 10 for Kashmir.

Calling for greater investment in digitalisation and capacity building, the Minister emphasised smart-grid technologies, cybersecurity, modern operational systems and specialised training for power-sector personnel.
He proposed establishing two dedicated Power Training Colleges, one each in the Jammu and Kashmir divisions.

Sagar said reliable and affordable electricity was essential for supporting industrial growth, tourism, horticulture, cold-chain infrastructure, healthcare facilities and the emerging electric mobility ecosystem in Jammu and Kashmir.

He urged the Centre to consider a dedicated Jammu and Kashmir Power Sector Development and Modernisation Package, combining grants, concessional loans, viability gap funding and project-based assistance.

The Minister also proposed constitution of a joint working group comprising representatives of the Government of India and Jammu and Kashmir to examine the proposals and facilitate their time-bound implementation.
